records.place: Liberty Bell Center, Independence National Historical Park
records.founder: John Pass and John Stow, Philadelphia (1753 recast)
records.foundry: Whitechapel Foundry, London (first casting, 1752); recast in Philadelphia
records.history: The first bell was cast in 1752 by Thomas Lester and Thomas Pack at the Whitechapel Foundry in London, and was recast twice in 1753 by John Pass and John Stow in Philadelphia. The surviving bell is that 1753 recast. It was the State House bell, ordered to call lawmakers and townspeople. The official history page states there is no evidence that it rang on 4 or 8 July 1776. In 1846 a repair of an earlier crack failed; a second fissure silenced the bell.
records.status: Silenced after a second fissure in 1846
records.title: Liberty Bell
records.coordinate_source: OpenStreetMap way 40086417, Liberty Bell Center. https://www.openstreetmap.org/way/40086417

records.place: Benjamin Rush Garden, Independence National Historical Park
records.history: Cast in 1976 (the inscription date on the official page is 4 July 1976) and presented on 6 July 1976 as a gift from the people of Britain to the people of the United States for the 200th anniversary of American independence. The inscription includes “LET FREEDOM RING.” It previously rang from a tower in the park.
records.title: Bicentennial Bell
records.coordinate_source: OpenStreetMap way 1302753999, Benjamin Rush Garden. https://www.openstreetmap.org/way/1302753999

records.place: Independence Hall tower, Independence National Historical Park
records.history: First rang to mark the nation’s 100th birthday in 1876. It hangs in the same spot the Liberty Bell once did. The visitor page says it has been struck with a mechanical hammer since 1926 and still rings hourly. Coordinates are the USGS GNIS August 2021 archive feature for Independence Hall (Feature ID 1177722).

records.place: Washington Memorial Chapel, Valley Forge, Pennsylvania
records.foundry: Meneely Bell Foundry (Meneely Bell Co.), Troy, New York
records.history: Also called the Women’s Liberty Bell or Suffrage Bell on the NPS page. A near replica of the Liberty Bell, cast without a crack in 1915 (the inscription date MCMXV) and used in the women’s suffrage campaign. Its clapper was chained so it could not ring, then it was rung 48 times after ratification of the 19th Amendment in August 1920. It is on permanent display at Washington Memorial Chapel. Coordinates are the USGS GNIS August 2021 archive feature Washington Memorial Church (Feature ID 1190629).

The page says the bell was designed in 1991 and dedicated in 1996, and presents it as a symbol of peace and reconciliation. Visitors are encouraged to ring it in times of celebration and remembrance.

records.place: Belfry of Elizabeth Tower, Palace of Westminster, United Kingdom
records.foundry: Whitechapel Bell Foundry, East London (present bell); first bell: Warners of Norton
records.history: A first bell was cast in 1856 at Warners of Norton, near Stockton-on-Tees, and cracked in testing in 1857. The present bell was cast in April 1858 at the Whitechapel Bell Foundry. Its strikes were first heard on 11 July 1859; later that year it was found fractured and was silent until 1863, when it was turned 90 degrees and the hammer reduced. BBC Radio first broadcast the chimes on New Year’s Eve 1923. After a 5 August 1976 clock failure it was silent for nearly nine months and rang again in May 1977. The present bell is fixed and struck from outside. Historic England lists a National Grid Reference for Elizabeth Tower; the map pin uses the OpenStreetMap Elizabeth Tower building coordinate, not a conversion of that grid reference.
records.title: Great Bell of the Great Clock (commonly called Big Ben)
records.coordinate_source: OpenStreetMap way 123557148, Elizabeth Tower (building coordinate; not a conversion of the Historic England National Grid Reference). https://www.openstreetmap.org/way/123557148

records.place: National Museum of Ireland (Treasury), on display
records.history: The official artefact page dates the iron bell to the 8th–9th century AD and the shrine to circa AD 1100. The page names craftsmen only on the later shrine inscription; the founder of the iron bell itself is Unknown. The bell is reputed to have belonged to St Patrick and is frequently mentioned in written sources as one of the principal relics of Ireland. It is made of two riveted iron sheets coated with bronze.
records.title: The Bell of St Patrick (and its shrine)
records.coordinate_source: OpenStreetMap way 1029441205, National Museum of Ireland, Archaeology, Kildare Street. https://www.openstreetmap.org/way/1029441205

records.place: United Nations Headquarters, exterior grounds
records.history: Cast in 1952 and presented to the United Nations on 8 June 1954. The official gift record says it is traditionally rung twice a year: on the first day of spring (vernal equinox / Earth Day) and on the opening day of the General Assembly in September (International Day of Peace). Coordinates are the USGS GNIS August 2021 archive feature United Nations Headquarters (Feature ID 968243), the Headquarters building, not a separate Peace Bell feature.
records.title: Japanese Peace Bell

records.place: South tower, cathedral of Notre-Dame de Paris
records.founder: Florentin II Le Guay, with Nicolas Chapelle, Jean Gillot, and François Moreau (third and present pour)
records.history: The official page records three pours, on 17 September 1680, 31 October 1681, and 4 March 1686; the successful third pour is the present bourdon, blessed 29 April 1686. Classified as a historic monument by order of 24 July 1944. Removed in 1794 and put back for the Concordat ceremony on 18 April 1802. The present 1686 bell sounded at the service for Louis XIV on 28 October 1715.

The same page dates the bell tower itself to 1207–1210 and lists it as a National Treasure. Weight 26.3 tons. The page calls it one of the Three Famous Bells of Japan and says it is known for its long ring.

records.history: The official collection record dates it “c 1800-1899” and says it was “cast in the nineteenth century for a wooden boat.” Maker is listed as Unknown; place made, Germany. Later presented by the city of Emden to SMS Emden when that ship was commissioned in 1909; removed from the wreck by the Royal Australian Navy after the action with HMAS Sydney (I) on 9 November 1914 and retained as a war trophy. The record also states naval bells are used for signalling, timekeeping, alarms, and ceremony.

records.history: The official cathedral bells page calls it the largest bell in the UK in current use, 16.75 imperial tons, note E flat, and the second largest bell ever cast in the British Isles. For about 30 years it was chimed daily with an automated mechanism, which the page says is broken; it is now rung manually for special occasions such as major services and the Lord Mayor’s Show.

records.place: South-west tower, St Paul’s Cathedral, London, among the three clock bells
records.founder: Richard Phelps of the Whitechapel Foundry
records.history: The official page calls it the largest of the cathedral’s three clock bells, over 5 tons, in A flat, and the successor to a much older bell acquired from the Palace of Westminster in 1698, which was cracked in transit. It strikes the hours and is tolled manually to mark the deaths of senior members of the Royal Family or, should they die in office, the Archbishop of Canterbury, the Bishop of London, the Dean of St Paul’s, the Lord Mayor of London, or the Prime Minister. The page says this was last done in September 2025, and before that upon the death of Queen Elizabeth II.

records.place: South tower of Cologne Cathedral, about 53 m up
records.history: The inscription gives 1922, as originally planned, but the official page says the bell was cast in Apolda on the evening of 5 May 1923. Bronze; strike note c0. Until the end of the 20th century it was the largest free-swinging bell in the world. It replaced the Kaiserglocke (cast 1874 by Andreas Hamm in Frankenthal), taken apart between May and July 1918 for wartime metal. Blessed 30 November 1924; a first ringing on Christmas Eve 1924 failed; it was first heard on 28 October 1925. It rings on high church feasts and special occasions.

records.place: Colle di Miravalle, Rovereto, Italy
records.foundry: Capanni foundry, Castelnovo Né Monti (1964 recast); foundry names for the 1924 and 1939 casts are Unknown
records.history: The official foundation page: first cast in Trento on 30 October 1924 from bronze of cannons donated by nations involved in the First World War; recast in Verona on 13 June 1939; the present bell was recast on 1 August 1964 at the Capanni foundry, Castelnovo Né Monti. Conceived in Rovereto to honour the fallen of all wars and to invoke peace and brotherhood. Baptised “Maria Dolens” in Rovereto on 24 May 1925 and inaugurated 4 October 1925. A crack stopped it ringing on 31 August 1960. Placed at Colle di Miravalle, near the Castel Dante Ossuary, on 4 November 1965 (earlier, after the 1925 inauguration, it stood on the Malipiero Bastion of Rovereto Castle). The page calls it the world’s largest swinging bell and says it has sounded every evening for over eighty years to commemorate the fallen, without distinction of faith or nationality. Blessed in St Peter’s Square, Rome, on 31 October 1965.
records.title: Maria Dolens (Campana dei Caduti / Bell of the Fallen)
records.coordinate_source: OpenStreetMap node 270099585, Campana dei Caduti, Rovereto. https://www.openstreetmap.org/node/270099585
